summary: Paul opens with a claim of apostleship that comes from neither people nor any person, greets the Galatian assemblies, then moves at once to alarm: they are deserting the one who called them for a distorted version of the Good News, and any messenger who alters it stands cursed. The rest of the chapter is his own story — persecutor, called by God's pleasure, three years unknown to Jerusalem — told to prove his message came by revelation, not inheritance.
whyItMatters: This chapter sets the terms of the whole letter: there is one Good News, it was not Paul's own editing of Jerusalem's version, and altering it is not a small difference of emphasis but a desertion. Everything Paul argues later rests on the claim he stakes here.

context.author: Paul, writing with 'all the brothers who are with me' (1:2), names himself an apostle 'not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ' — a claim the whole chapter exists to defend.
context.audience: The assemblies of Galatia (1:2) — Gentile believers Paul had taught, now hearing a rival version of the message.
context.date: The letter itself dates nothing except Paul's own timeline — his calling, three years, then Damascus (1:15-18); scholarship places the letter in the middle of the first century, and the year depends on which Galatia and which Jerusalem visit (see the book briefing's debates).
context.setting: Written to assemblies Paul planted, after messengers arrived preaching a 'good news' Paul calls a distortion (1:7); the letter is his response to that news.
context.literaryForm: A letter that breaks convention: it skips the thanksgiving ancient letters carried and moves from greeting (1:1-5) straight to rebuke (1:6-9), then a narrative defense of Paul's commission (1:10-24).

outline.heading: Greeting with an edge already in it
outline.note: Paul's apostleship is disclaimed from human sources in the first line; the greeting wishes grace and peace and grounds them in Christ's self-giving 'according to the will of our God and Father.'

outline.heading: The alarm and the curse
outline.note: Paul marvels at their quick desertion, denies there is another Good News, and twice curses any messenger — himself or an angel — who alters the one they received; pleasing men and serving Christ are set against each other.

outline.heading: The Good News came by revelation
outline.note: The claim the chapter defends: the message was 'not according to man'; Paul did not receive or learn it, it came 'through revelation of Jesus Christ.'

outline.heading: The persecutor's former life
outline.note: Paul's own resume, told against himself: he persecuted the assembly of God beyond measure and advanced in Judaism past his contemporaries, zealous for ancestral traditions.

outline.heading: Called, and deliberately not consulting Jerusalem
outline.note: God set him apart from the womb and called him by grace; instead of conferring with anyone or going up to Jerusalem, he went away into Arabia and back to Damascus.

outline.heading: Three years, one visit, two names
outline.note: Only after three years does Paul visit Peter for fifteen days, seeing no other apostle except James; the Judean assemblies had never met him, and they glorified God because the persecutor now preached the faith he had tried to destroy.

keyVerses.text: Paul, an apostle—not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ, and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—
keyVerses.why: The letter's first line is the thesis of its first half: Paul's commission and thus his message do not derive from any human chain of authority.

keyVerses.text: But even though we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you any “good news” other than that which we preached to you, let him be cursed.
keyVerses.why: The boundary is drawn to include Paul himself; the message judges the messenger, not the other way around.

keyVerses.text: For I didn’t receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ.
keyVerses.why: The positive claim behind the chapter's narrative: revelation, not instruction, is the source of the Good News Paul preaches.

themes: one Good News and its distortions

questions.question: Why does Paul call himself an apostle 'not from men, nor through man'?
questions.answer: The rival teachers in Galatia seem to have undercut Paul as secondhand — not one of the original apostles, so his gospel suspect (see 1:1 alongside 1:11-12). He answers by tracing his commission past Jerusalem entirely: God set him apart from the womb, called him by grace, and revealed the Son to him — so his message has the same kind of source as the apostles': Christ, not a chain of human training.

questions.question: What does 'deserting' mean in verse 6?
questions.answer: The hosted text says they are 'so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ' — the verb means transferring allegiance. The desertion is not described as switching churches but as leaving God himself, because the alternative message substitutes requirements for grace.

questions.question: Does Paul really say a person can be cursed for preaching?
questions.answer: The word is 'anathema' — devoted to destruction — and Paul applies it to any messenger who alters the Good News, explicitly including himself and angels (1:8-9). The point is how serious the alteration is: a changed message un-changes the gospel. Readers differ on how far to press the word today; within the letter it functions as the extreme boundary marker of a single-message claim.

questions.question: Why is there no thanksgiving in the opening, like Paul's other letters?
questions.answer: Ancient letters normally included a thanksgiving or blessing for the recipients after the greeting; Paul's letters usually carry one. Here 1:6 turns directly to alarm — 'I marvel that you are so quickly deserting.' The missing section is a deliberate signal of the emergency, not an oversight.

questions.question: What was Paul's life like before this letter's story begins?
questions.answer: He says he persecuted the assembly of God 'beyond measure' and ravaged it, advancing in Judaism past many of his contemporaries, 'more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers' (1:13-14). The point of the resume is contrast: the man now defending Gentile freedom was the movement's most aggressive opponent.

questions.question: Why does Paul insist he did not go to Jerusalem right away?
questions.answer: The argument needs his message to be independent of the apostles', not derived from them. So he reports that after his calling he did not confer with anyone, went to Arabia, returned to Damascus, and only visited Jerusalem three years later — and then saw only Peter for fifteen days and James (1:16-19). His gospel cannot be a Jerusalem edition if he was not there to receive one.

questions.question: Who is James, 'the Lord's brother,' in verse 19?
questions.answer: The letter names him without explanation, as a known figure. Readers differ over exactly how this James relates to Jesus's family — the phrase most plainly reads as a brother in the ordinary sense, while later traditions propose other relationships — but the letter's own use of him is fixed: he is one of only two named figures Paul saw in Jerusalem at that visit, and he later appears among the 'pillars' (2:9).

questions.question: Why does Paul swear 'before God, I'm not lying'?
questions.answer: The oath at 1:20 guards the part of the story most likely to be challenged: that he saw no apostle except James during those three years and that visit of fifteen days. It is a courtroom move in a chapter built like a defense — he is establishing an alibi of independence for his gospel.

questions.question: What does Arabia have to do with anything?
questions.answer: Paul reports going away into Arabia before returning to Damascus (1:17) and gives no reason. The letter uses the trip as a fact in the independence argument — he went away rather than up to Jerusalem — and nothing more; what he did there is not stated, so any further story about it comes from outside the letter.

glossary.def: A sent one with a commission; Paul claims the title on the grounds that his commission came from Christ and God directly, not from any human body.
The hosted translation's rendering of euangelion, elsewhere 'gospel'; the letter's word for the single message it defends against alteration.
The hosted text's word for a local gathering of believers; Paul persecuted 'the assembly of God' and writes to 'the assemblies of Galatia.'
